# Simulation

Making a shape behave. Three stacks live here and they answer different questions.

**`afield.simulation.physics` is the one that moves.** It is a CPU solver you step inside your own `loop { }`, at frame rate, with a person's hand on it: `SimdVerlet` holds some thousands of particles in flat float arrays and pulls them together with distance constraints, and on top of that sit `Cloth`, `Strand`, `Wind`, tearing and a collider set. `JoltPhysicsWorld` is the rigid-body half — boxes, spheres, meshes, joints and character controllers over the Jolt engine — and `Dyn4jScene` is the same idea flat, in 2D. Nothing here owns a renderer: every one of them hands back `FLine`s and where those go is your business. Nothing here needs a GPU either. It is fast and it is approximate, and the number it gives you is not a number you would put in a report.

**`afield.simulation.kratos` is the one that is right.** It is finite elements, out of process: `KratosSession` starts a Python worker — a local venv, a container, or one already running — and talks to it over an authenticated socket, so nothing in Field's own startup imports a solver and a machine without the optional environment simply says so. A solve is seconds, not milliseconds, which is why the Kratos examples put it behind a button. What you get back is a `SimulationResult`, which describes its own fields rather than declaring them, so one class carries a scalar temperature and a velocity–pressure pair without knowing about either. The layer above it is the reason to care: a `StudySpace` varies the design, a `measure` reduces each answer to one number, and `KratosStudy` reports the landscape and where its optimum lies. Because the embedded formulations reclassify one fixed background grid instead of remeshing, **geometry is an ordinary study axis** — sweeping an arm length costs what sweeping a conductivity costs. `KratosStudyFigure` draws the result as pixels a box can display.

**`afield.geometry.mesh.tetgen` is the one in between.** Kratos has no embedded structural element, so stress needs a mesh whose boundary really is the part's surface, sharp edges included. `Tetgen.tetrahedralize` takes a closed triangle surface — a [Manifold](../manifold.md) solid, usually — and fills it with tetrahedra that reproduce it exactly, optionally quadratic, in Kratos's own node order. `TetMeshViews` is how you look at the inside of the result rather than at its skin.

Where the neighbours are. [Solvers](solvers.md) is Ceres, which finds the shape you *want* by minimising residuals you declare; simulation tells you what that shape then *does*. A gridshell relaxed in `Solvers` and a bracket solved in Kratos are two halves of the same design loop, not two ways of doing one thing. Everything above returns geometry, so [Graphics](graphics.md) is where it gets drawn.

The prose, with pictures: [Physics: particles, constraints and cloth](../physics.md) for the real-time stack — read it before touching `stiffness`, because it and `iterations` are not two knobs — and [Filling a solid: tetrahedral meshing with TetGen](../tetgen.md) for the meshing and the route into Kratos. Four loadable Kratos documents (thermal, flow, structural and the parameter study) and the cloth starting point are in the [Agent Transcript Gallery](../agent_transcripts.md); [Frames and the Animation Loop](../animation_time_model.md) explains why an integrator wants a fixed `dt`. `dev_docs/TETGEN.md` carries the mesher comparison that chose this route.

## Score.kt { #score-kt }

The canvas as a score: boxes are the events, a playhead box sweeps across them, and each box's
`score { }` runs every frame the playhead is over it.

A box arms itself with [`score`](simulation.md#score-kt--score); the lead box starts the clock with [`playScore`](simulation.md#score-kt--playscore), which moves the
box named `playhead` across a horizontal span of the canvas once per `loop` seconds and calls every
armed box whose frame the playhead crosses. Inside `score { }` the receiver is a [`ScoreFrame`](simulation.md#score-kt-scoreframe): how
far through the box the playhead is ([`ScoreFrame.localProgress`](simulation.md#score-kt--scoreframe--localprogress), [`ScoreFrame.localT`](simulation.md#score-kt--scoreframe--localt)), whether it
just arrived ([`ScoreFrame.justEntered`](simulation.md#score-kt--scoreframe--justentered)), a [`ScoreFrame.draw`](simulation.md#score-kt--scoreframe--draw) list that the lead box's output panel
shows as a canvas, dough sound ([`ScoreFrame.sound`](simulation.md#score-kt--scoreframe--sound)) and the box's measured level
([`ScoreFrame.thisRMS`](simulation.md#score-kt--scoreframe--thisrms)), and the box's own frame ([`ScoreFrame.box`](simulation.md#score-kt--scoreframe--box)), which it may move.

This is Field's time slider (`templates/timeSlider`: a line box that starts the boxes it passes
over) with a clock and per-frame calls instead of launches, so a box's code is compiled once, when
it is run, rather than every time the playhead reaches it. The clock is [`AnimationClock`](workspace.md#runloop-kt-animationclock), so a
video recording of a score plays at the right speed.

## movement.kt { #movement-kt }

Springs, dampers, and a steerable character built out of four of them.

Two layers, and the lower one is useful alone. [`Springs`](simulation.md#movement-kt-springs) holds the primitives as one-line
functions over `Float` and `Vector2f`: exponential dampers, critically damped springs, an angle
spring that takes the short way round, and the decay that hides a jump. [`MovementState`](simulation.md#movement-kt-movementstate) stacks
four of those into a character with a position, a velocity and a facing, driven by a desired
velocity and tuned through [`MovementParams`](simulation.md#movement-kt-movementparams).

Half-life is the parameter throughout: the time a spring takes to close half the distance to its
goal. That is what makes these tunable by eye, rather than by bisecting a stiffness against a
damping ratio. Every step is the analytic solution of the spring's equation rather than a
numerical integration, so one step of `dt` and ten steps of `dt / 10` land in the same place and
the motion does not change with frame rate.

All of it is plain arithmetic on the CPU, with no renderer and no solver underneath. Both layers
follow Daniel Holden's ["Spring-It-On"](https://theorangeduck.com/page/spring-roll-call) and
["A New Movement Model"](https://theorangeduck.com/page/new-movement-model).

## TetMeshViews.kt { #tetmeshviews-kt }

Ways of looking at a [`TetMesh`](simulation.md#tetgen-kt-tetmesh): its element quality, a slice of it, and the triangles that draw it.

A tetrahedral mesh has an inside, which is the whole point of it and also the reason it is awkward
to look at. Rendering one naively draws the boundary and hides everything the mesher actually did.
The three answers here are the three that get used: [`boundary`](simulation.md#tetmeshviews-kt--boundary) for the outside, [`filtered`](simulation.md#tetmeshviews-kt--filtered) with a
half-space predicate for a cutaway, and [`toTriMesh`](simulation.md#tetmeshviews-kt--totrimesh) with `shrink` below 1 for a shrunken-element
view where each tetrahedron is visibly its own cell.

The two quality measures are kept apart because they answer different questions, and they are
easily confused:

- [`radiusEdgeRatios`](simulation.md#tetmeshviews-kt--radiusedgeratios) is what TetGen's `-q` switch bounds, and therefore the number to check when
  you want to know whether the mesher honoured what you asked for.
- [`qualities`](simulation.md#tetmeshviews-kt--qualities) is the radius ratio, which is what a solver's conditioning cares about. TetGen does
  not bound it, and it is the number that detects a sliver.

All of these read a cell's first four indices and ignore the rest, so a 10-node mesh from
[`TetMesh.quadratic`](simulation.md#tetgen-kt--tetmesh--quadratic) measures and draws exactly as its 4-node original does. The six midside nodes
sit at the midpoints of straight edges, so the region, the boundary and every quality measure are
the same. What the extra nodes change is the interpolation inside an element, which none of these
views is looking at.

## Tetgen.kt { #tetgen-kt }

A closed surface turned into tetrahedra, with its sharp edges intact.

This is the discretisation half of the Kratos bridge for **body-fitted** work. The embedded
formulations (`thermal.stationary`, `flow.embedded`) never come here: they sample a level set
onto a fixed background grid and cut with it. Structural mechanics has no embedded element in
Kratos, so it needs a mesh whose boundary really is the part's surface — and, more to the point,
whose boundary reproduces the part's *edges*, because that is where stress concentrates.

### Why not the level-set route

`dev_docs/TETGEN.md` has the measurement in full. The short version, on the same body at the same
element size:

| | MMG, level set | TetGen, this |
|---|---|---|
| time | 4669 ms | 223 ms |
| boundary error, curved surface | 0.55 h | 0.024 h |
| boundary error, a box's edges | 0.35–0.40 h, at every resolution | **exactly 0** |

Sampling an SDF onto grid nodes destroys a sharp edge before the mesher ever sees it, and
refining only buys a smaller rounded radius. TetGen is handed the Manifold triangulation itself,
whose edges are exact, and constrains its output to it.

### Why there is no incremental meshing

A full re-tetrahedralization of a realistic body is ~0.2 s here. Against a Kratos structural
solve that is noise, so a geometry edit simply re-meshes. No part of this tries to update a mesh
in place.

## alife_vehicles.kt { #alife-vehicles-kt }

Braitenberg vehicles whose neurons have internal state: two light sensors, two motor neurons,
two wheels, and between them a small dynamical system rather than a wire.

In Braitenberg's book a vehicle's wiring is its personality: crossed excitatory wires make an
"aggressor" that speeds into a light, uncrossed inhibitory wires make a "lover" that slows down and
parks in front of it. Those vehicles are memoryless — the wheel speed is a function of what the
sensors read *now*. Here each motor neuron carries three kinds of memory on three timescales:

- **membrane** (a few steps): a leaky integrator, so the vehicle responds to a smoothed input;
- **hysteresis** (state-dependent): self-excitation, which makes a steep activation bistable, so a
  neuron that switched on at one input level switches off at a lower one;
- **homeostasis** (hundreds of steps, [`NeuronParams.adaptationRate`](simulation.md#alife-vehicles-kt--neuronparams--adaptationrate)): the threshold integrates the
  difference between the neuron's rate and a target rate, so a vehicle held in constant light gets
  used to it — a parked lover eventually drives off;
- **plasticity** (thousands of steps, [`PlasticityParams`](simulation.md#alife-vehicles-kt-plasticityparams)): the four sensor→motor weights learn from
  reward-modulated eligibility traces of the motor noise, so a randomly wired population can
  discover, on its own, that crossed wiring brings it into the light.

Each of these is switched off by one parameter, which is how the measurements on the docs page
make their claims: same seed, one ingredient removed, a number that changes.

Mutable, like [`BoidFlock`](alife.md#alife-agents-kt-boidflock): [`VehicleWorld.step`](simulation.md#alife-vehicles-kt--vehicleworld--step) advances the population in place.

| <a id="alife-vehicles-kt--orbitbias"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">orbitBias</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">distance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">weight</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">2.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">light</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Light</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Light</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_vehicles/#L306) | The [`NeuronParams.bias`](simulation.md#alife-vehicles-kt--neuronparams--bias) that makes an `Activation.BUMP` neuron fire hardest when a sensor wired with `weight` reads the brightness `distance` away from `light`. Wired crossed and excitatory (`VehicleWorld.AGGRESSOR`), such a vehicle turns toward the light when it is farther than `distance` and away from it when nearer, so it circles at about that radius. |

## Creatures.kt { #creatures-kt }

Evolving 2D creatures: a genetic algorithm over bodies of points and springs whose every point is a foot
with a cyclic contact program, and whose joints are angle motors following cyclic target curves.

[`CreatureEvolution.evolve`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creatureevolution--evolve) (or [`CreatureEvolution.evolveFlow`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creatureevolution--evolveflow)) breeds a population under an
[`EvolutionConfig`](simulation.md#creatures-kt-evolutionconfig); [`CreatureEvolution.simulate`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creatureevolution--simulate) scores one [`CreatureGenome`](simulation.md#creatures-kt-creaturegenome); a [`CreatureEvaluation`](simulation.md#creatures-kt-creatureevaluation) plays
back as FLines ([`CreatureEvaluation.frameLines`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creatureevaluation--framelines)) with a per-foot score ([`CreatureEvaluation.notationLines`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creatureevaluation--notationlines)).

The world is not in here. A [`ContactModel`](simulation.md#creatures-kt-contactmodel) says what a foot receives from its surroundings, and
[`CreatureSimulationConfig.fitness`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creaturesimulationconfig--fitness) says what counts as doing well, so a water strider, a crawler on a
floor and a swimmer differ only in box code. The `evolving_water_bugs` starting point writes two of
those contact models.

One thing to know before writing a [`CreatureSimulationConfig.fitness`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creaturesimulationconfig--fitness): during selection it is handed an
evaluation with no frames. Evolution scores its whole population with recording off and re-simulates
only each generation's best under the configured recording, so a score read out of
[`CreatureEvaluation.frames`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creatureevaluation--frames) is zero for every creature that is actually being chosen between. Score
from the measured totals instead — [`CreatureEvaluation.sustainedTravel`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creatureevaluation--sustainedtravel),
[`CreatureEvaluation.displacement`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creatureevaluation--displacement) and the means beside them.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/creatures/Creatures.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/creatures/Creatures/)

**Used in:** [Evolving Creatures](../evolving_creatures.md)

### EdgeGene { #creatures-kt-edgegene }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">EdgeGene</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/creatures/Creatures/#L95)

One spring of the body, as the indices of the two points it joins. Its rest length is whatever the distance between those points is in [`CreatureGenome.points`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creaturegenome--points), so the rest shape and the springs are the same piece of genome.

### ContactProgram { #creatures-kt-contactprogram }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ContactProgram</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">phase</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">duty</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.35f</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">smooth</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.2f</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">strength</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1f</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/creatures/Creatures/#L110)

One foot's gait, as a window on the body's phase clock: the foot is down over [`duty`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--contactprogram--duty) of each cycle, centred on `phase`, pressing with [`strength`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--contactprogram--strength). Every point of a creature carries one of these, and [`CreatureGenome.feet`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creaturegenome--feet) is parallel to [`CreatureGenome.points`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--creaturegenome--points).

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">JointProgram</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">pivot</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">targets</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">JOINT&#95;TARGET&#95;KNOT&#95;COUNT</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">{</span> <span class="mi">0f</span> <span class="p">}</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/creatures/Creatures/#L142)

An angle motor at [`pivot`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--jointprogram--pivot), pulling the angle between its two neighbours [`a`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--jointprogram--a) and [`b`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--jointprogram--b) toward a target that cycles with the phase clock. ### ContactModel { #creatures-kt-contactmodel }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">ContactModel</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/creatures/Creatures/#L383)

The environment a creature moves in, as the force each foot receives. Every point of the body is a foot (most of them evolve programs that never touch down), and each gets its own [`Foot`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--contactmodel--foot-2) from [`foot`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--contactmodel--foot), so a foot can remember where it planted.

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">CreatureSnapshot</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">step</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">phase</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">center</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">points</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Float2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">down</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Boolean</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">anchors</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Float2</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">jointTorques</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">jointTargets</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/creatures/Creatures/#L434)

### EvolutionGeneration { #creatures-kt-evolutiongeneration }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">EvolutionGeneration</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">generation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">bestFitness</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">meanFitness</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">medianFitness</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/creatures/Creatures/#L893)

The fitness spread of one finished generation, over the genomes that survived repair. A genome no repair could make valid is dropped rather than scored, so these are computed over a population that can be smaller than [`EvolutionConfig.populationSize`](simulation.md#creatures-kt--evolutionconfig--populationsize).

## FlowShaders.kt { #flowshaders-kt }

Packaged GLSL helpers (`grain.glsl`, `strokes.glsl`, `motion.glsl`, `tiles.glsl`) for flow
shaders, reachable as `#include "flow/..."`.

The include resolver in `shaders.kt` already falls back to [`FlowShaders.source`](simulation.md#flowshaders-kt--flowshaders--source) for `flow/`
paths, so a document needs no setup; [`FlowShaders.install`](simulation.md#flowshaders-kt--flowshaders--install) registers the root explicitly,
replacing any custom `flow` registration. Passes, resources and artistic controls stay in
editable boxes.

## TileAtlasLayout.kt { #tileatlaslayout-kt }

Maps tile slots of a [`afield.graphics.render.TileResidency`](simulation.md#tileresidency-kt-tileresidency) onto pixel coordinates in one GPU
atlas texture, with a halo border around each tile.

Each slot occupies a square of `cellsPerTile + 2 * halo` pixels, laid out in the residency's
columns and rows. [`TileAtlasLayout.pixelX`](simulation.md#tileatlaslayout-kt--tileatlaslayout--pixelx) and [`TileAtlasLayout.pixelY`](simulation.md#tileatlaslayout-kt--tileatlaslayout--pixely) address a cell inside a
slot (negative cells and cells past the tile reach into the halo), and
[`TileAtlasLayout.updateHeaders`](simulation.md#tileatlaslayout-kt--tileatlaslayout--updateheaders) packs four ints per slot (world tile x and y, generation,
occupied) for upload. The layout owns no textures and schedules no work. Halos are meant to be
filled from resident neighbouring tiles rather than by wrapping atlas coordinates, so the layout
implies no periodic world boundary.

## KratosDemo.kt { #kratosdemo-kt }

The two Kratos smoke runs, and the small piece of geometry they share.

Both are `jvm-main` entry points rather than unit tests, because both need a worker process.
Each asks `Kratos.probeAny` for whichever launch this machine can actually run and prints a
passing line naming what was missing when the answer is none, so a checkout with no Kratos
installed still runs them green. Both read their startup budget off the resolved launch, since a
container under x86-64 emulation takes far longer to reach its first frame than a native venv.

`kratos.embedded.thermal` covers the embedded route: one session over a fixed box, a committed
solve of [`KratosDemo.body`](simulation.md#kratosdemo-kt--kratosdemo--body), then two preview solves with a shorter arm. What it establishes is
the pair of claims the route is for — that a geometric change is a reclassification of the same
[`BackgroundDomain`](simulation.md#simulationgeometry-kt-backgrounddomain) instance rather than a remesh, with `buildCount` still 1 and the temperatures
moved; and that a preview overtaken by a later edit completes with null instead of arriving late.

`kratos.structural.quadratic` covers the body-fitted route, and it checks physics rather than
plumbing: the same cantilever meshed at both tetrahedron orders, against the Euler-Bernoulli tip
deflection of a uniformly loaded beam. It skips when TetGen or Manifold is absent, because
body-fitted meshing goes through both.

## KratosLaunch.kt { #kratoslaunch-kt }

Where the Kratos worker process comes from, and which end of the socket Field owns.

The protocol above this is identical in all three cases: one authenticated frame stream, one
session, the envelope described in `optional/kratos/protocol.md`. What differs is everything
before the first frame.

| | who runs Python | who listens | who dials |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LocalProcess` | Field, as a child process | Field, on an ephemeral 127.0.0.1 port | the worker |
| `Container` | Field, as a container | the worker, inside its namespace | Field, on the published port |
| `Attach` | nobody, it is already running | the worker | Field |

### Why the container case reverses the direction

`LocalProcess` binds `127.0.0.1` in the JVM and hands the port to the child, which connects back.
A container cannot do that. Its network namespace is not the host's, so the host's loopback
interface is not reachable from inside it, and on macOS there is a virtual machine in between as
well. Publishing a port is the direction that *does* work through both, so in `Container` the
worker binds and Field dials.

That does mean the worker binds `0.0.0.0`, inside the container. Only the port the runtime
publishes leaves that namespace, and it is published to `127.0.0.1` on the host, so the host's
exposure is the same loopback-only socket either way. The token is checked on the first frame in
both directions.

### Why the container launch exists at all

Kratos publishes `manylinux_2_28_x86_64` and `win_amd64` wheels. There is no macOS wheel for
either architecture, so on an Apple Silicon checkout `uv sync --project optional/kratos` fails
during resolution and `LocalProcess` has nothing to run. The container carries the same pinned
environment, resolved from the same `uv.lock`. Under emulation it is slow enough that the
measured component times mean nothing as absolute numbers; the ratios between them still do.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/kratos/KratosLaunch.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/kratos/KratosLaunch/)

## KratosSession.kt { #kratossession-kt }

The JVM side of the Kratos link: finding a worker, opening a session on it, and asking for solves.

The physics does not run in this process. A Kratos solve runs in a Python worker reached over one
authenticated socket, and nothing in this file imports native solver code, so a checkout with no
Kratos installed still starts and still compiles. Whether a solve can actually happen is a
runtime question, and [`Kratos`](simulation.md#kratossession-kt-kratos) is where it is asked: `probe` starts one worker, `probeAny` tries
each launch this machine could plausibly use and reports which one answered, and `howToInstall`
says what is missing in terms of the platform asking. Kratos publishes Linux and Windows wheels
only, so on macOS there is nothing a `uv sync` could install and the container launch is the only
route to a solve; advice that did not know the platform would be advice to run a command that
cannot succeed.

### The formulation is the only thing that knows any physics

[`SimulationParameters`](simulation.md#kratossession-kt-simulationparameters) is the physics half of a request: a registry name the worker recognises,
and the coefficients that go with it. [`ThermalParameters`](simulation.md#kratossession-kt-thermalparameters), [`FlowParameters`](simulation.md#kratossession-kt-flowparameters) and
[`StructuralParameters`](simulation.md#kratossession-kt-structuralparameters) are the three implemented here. Everything else in the file (the launch,
the framing, the binary arrays, revisions, cancellation) never looks at which formulation is
running, and [`SimulationResult`](simulation.md#simulationresult-kt-simulationresult) decodes whatever field list the worker declares. Adding a physics
is therefore one more implementation of this interface beside one more worker-side formulation,
and no change to the transport.

### Two ways to open a session, and they are not interchangeable

`KratosSession.openAsync` gives the worker bounds and a resolution and lets it build a structured
background grid; geometry is then classified against that grid, which is what makes a geometric
change cheap. `KratosSession.openMeshAsync` sends a tetrahedral mesh Field has already made with
`afield.geometry.mesh.tetgen.Tetgen`, for a formulation that solves the mesh it was given. `isBodyFitted`
reports which kind a session is, and it decides which `solveAsync` overload is legal: the
embedded one takes a [`SimulationGeometry`](simulation.md#simulationgeometry-kt-simulationgeometry) per solve, the body-fitted one refuses a geometry
because changing the mesh means opening a new session.

### Newest wins

A session is built for a slider. A new request immediately obsoletes the ones before it: the
simulation half of [`SimulationRevision`](simulation.md#kratossession-kt-simulationrevision) increments, and an obsoleted future completes `null`
rather than handing back a field that answers a superseded question. In-flight native
solves are left to finish and their results are dropped, since there is no way to interrupt
Kratos mid-solve. All of it runs off Field's runloop on one thread, so `withLatest` is how a draw
gets a result and the revision it belongs to without racing the next solve.

That policy is wrong for anything that needs every answer rather than the latest one, which is
why [`KratosStudy`](simulation.md#kratosstudy-kt-kratosstudy) drives a session strictly one solve at a time.

## KratosStudy.kt { #kratosstudy-kt }

Run one Kratos session many times over a declared design space, and compare the answers.

[`KratosSession`](simulation.md#kratossession-kt-kratossession) and the worker below it answer exactly one question: *given this geometry and
these coefficients, what is the field?* That is a simulator. A **study** is the layer that turns
it into a design tool. It varies the question, reduces each answer to one number, and reports the
shape of the resulting landscape and where its optimum lies.

A caller supplies three pieces:

- a [`StudySpace`](simulation.md#kratosstudy-kt-studyspace) — a base design object of any type `D` and the [`StudyVariable`](simulation.md#kratosstudy-kt-studyvariable)s that move it;
- a `plan`, mapping a design to the [`StudyCase`](simulation.md#kratosstudy-kt-studycase) the solver runs (geometry and coefficients);
- a `measure`, reducing a [`SimulationResult`](simulation.md#simulationresult-kt-simulationresult) to the scalar being optimised.

Keeping `plan` separate from `measure` is what lets **geometry be an ordinary axis**. For an
embedded formulation a geometric change is a reclassification of the same background grid, with
no remesh and no new session, so a sweep over an arm length costs what a sweep over a
conductivity costs and the two can be axes of one grid. The domain's `buildCount` stays 1 across
a whole sweep, and `KratosStudySmokeTest` fails if it does not. A body-fitted formulation has no
reclassification to do instead: [`evaluate`](simulation.md#kratosstudy-kt--kratosstudy--evaluate) refuses a [`StudyCase`](simulation.md#kratosstudy-kt-studycase) that carries a geometry there,
and a geometric axis needs a session per point rather than a study.

### One session solves one design at a time

[`KratosSession`](simulation.md#kratossession-kt-kratossession) is a newest-wins preview engine: a second `solveAsync` increments the simulation
revision and the first future then completes `null` rather than with a stale field. That is right
for a slider and wrong for a study, which needs *every* answer. So [`evaluate`](simulation.md#kratosstudy-kt--kratosstudy--evaluate) awaits each solve
before submitting the next, and the study's wall time is the sum of its solves. Submitting in
parallel against one session does not shorten it: the session obsoletes all but the last, and
each obsoleted solve arrives back here as a failed sample.

Two sessions do run two solves at once, at the cost of two workers and two background grids.

### Memoisation

Every evaluation is cached on a quantised coordinate signature, twelve significant figures per
coordinate, so re-running an overlapping grid (a refinement around the optimum, say) re-solves
only the points it has not seen. The cache is shared with [`optimise`](simulation.md#kratosstudy-kt--kratosstudy--optimise), and the search's own budget
accounting agrees with it because the [`GenomeOps`](search.md#populationsearch-kt-genomeops) implementation hands `PopulationSearch` that
same key.

### An infeasible design is a sample, not an exception

A design whose solve throws, or whose `measure` returns null because the probe fell outside the
solved region, becomes an **infeasible sample** carrying the reason instead of abandoning the
rest of the sweep. The [`StudySample`](simulation.md#kratosstudy-kt-studysample) holds that message in its `failure`, and [`fitnessOf`](simulation.md#kratosstudy-kt--kratosstudy--fitnessof) scores
such a sample as negative infinity, so a search treats it as the worst design it has seen rather
than stopping at it.

## KratosStudyFigure.kt { #kratosstudyfigure-kt }

A [`StudyLandscape`](simulation.md#kratosstudy-kt-studylandscape) and a [`StudyOptimisation`](simulation.md#kratosstudy-kt-studyoptimisation), as a picture.

A sweep's result is a table of numbers and a table of numbers is easy to be wrong about. What a
study is *for* is the shape: where the valley runs, whether the optimum is interior or pinned to
an edge, whether the search found the same place the grid did. All of that is one glance and none
of it is a summary line.

The raster is built on the CPU, through [`RasterImage`](visualization.md#heatmap-kt-rasterimage), with no AWT, no window and no GPU, so the
same code makes the figure inside a Field box, inside a `jvm-main` verification run and inside a
unit test. Text is drawn from the 3x5 dot-matrix font in `RectSL.kt`, so the repository has one
such table rather than a third copy of it. That font's alphabet is upper case, digits and a
handful of punctuation; labels are upper-cased on the way in, anything outside the alphabet draws
as a blank, and `drawable` is how a caller checks a label before the figure disappoints it.

### Reading the landscape panel

Axis 0 runs up the left edge and axis 1 along the bottom, which is the row-then-column reading
`StudyLandscape.matrix` returns. Cells are drawn as cells, with no bilinear smoothing, because a
study's resolution is a real property of the answer and a smoothed picture invents a landscape
between sample points that nobody solved. Infeasible points are hatched grey rather than coloured
zero. The grid's best cell gets a white ring, and an optimiser's best, when one is supplied, gets
a cross, so a reader can see where the two methods agree.

A study with one axis draws as a profile instead: the objective as a line across the panel, with
the infeasible points marked along the floor. Three axes or more are refused, naming the rank.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/kratos/KratosStudyFigure.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/kratos/KratosStudyFigure/)

## KratosStudyRun.kt { #kratosstudyrun-kt }

One parameter study over a heated part, in the three sizes a demo has to exist in.

[`KratosStudyDemo`](simulation.md#kratosstudyrun-kt-kratosstudydemo) is the experiment as a spec: the design space, the objective, the two reported
metrics and a closed-form check on the answer. It owns no runner of its own, because three things
have to agree on the same experiment: the full run below, the catalog smoke beside it, and the
loadable document in `dev_docs/agents/transcripts/kratos_parameter_study.yaml`. [`KratosStudyRun`](simulation.md#kratosstudyrun-kt-kratosstudyrun)
is that full run, driving a real Kratos worker through a coarse grid, a refinement seeded from
it, a global search against a random control, and finally the fine grid the figures are drawn
from. [`KratosStudySmokeTest`](simulation.md#kratosstudyrun-kt-kratosstudysmoketest) is the same code path at catalog size, and is the version the test
catalog runs.

The two design axes are one geometric (how far the arm extends) and one material (its
conductivity), and the study treats them identically. Because `thermal.stationary` is embedded,
moving the geometric axis reclassifies the same background grid rather than remeshing it: both
the full run and the smoke assert that the grid is built exactly once across a whole sweep, so a
sweep over a shape costs what a sweep over a coefficient costs.

The objective is one whose right answer is known in advance. Stationary conduction is
linear in the source and inverse in the conductivity, so the designs that put a target
temperature at a chosen point form a curve with a closed form, and
[`KratosStudyDemo.verifyValley`](simulation.md#kratosstudyrun-kt--kratosstudydemo--verifyvalley) holds every column of the sampled grid against it.

## SimulationGeometry.kt { #simulationgeometry-kt }

What a session is told about shape, and the discretisation that shape gets solved on.

Every [`SimulationGeometry`](simulation.md#simulationgeometry-kt-simulationgeometry) answers two questions, for two different readers.
`surface()` returns a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) for Field to draw, and Manifold builds that in every case.
`workerData(domain)` returns what goes over the wire, and the implementations answer it in two
different currencies.

### Symbolic, or sampled

A [`PrimitiveGeometry`](simulation.md#simulationgeometry-kt-primitivegeometry) sends `expression()`: a small tree of boxes, spheres, cylinders and boolean
operations that the worker evaluates as an exact distance at each node it cares about. A
[`ManifoldGeometry`](simulation.md#simulationgeometry-kt-manifoldgeometry) sends the distances themselves, one double per node of the domain, measured
against Field's own BVH over the triangulated solid and negated on the way out because Kratos
counts distance positive inside.

That difference decides what a display setting can and cannot affect. A primitive's tessellation
is a property of the picture only: refining a sphere's `segments` changes no node's
classification, because the worker never sees the triangles. For a [`ManifoldGeometry`](simulation.md#simulationgeometry-kt-manifoldgeometry) the
triangles are the input, so its payload is both sized to one particular domain's node count and
only as good as the mesh it was snapshotted from.

### Identity is authored, not derived

The `id` on a geometry is chosen by whoever built it and is independent of the triangle indices
Manifold happens to produce, which is what lets a boundary condition or a material keep naming
the same region across a re-solve: a formulation derives its region keys from that id.
[`SimulationGroup`](simulation.md#simulationgeometry-kt-simulationgroup) requires its operands' ids to be distinct for the same reason. Bounds are
metres, and coefficients are SI throughout, kelvin included.

### The domain is two different things behind one type

[`BackgroundDomain`](simulation.md#simulationgeometry-kt-backgrounddomain) is the node and cell arrays a result is indexed against, and its `resolution`
tells its two kinds apart. Positive means the worker built a structured Freudenthal grid from
[`SimulationBounds`](simulation.md#simulationgeometry-kt-simulationbounds), six tetrahedra to a cube, which is what makes sampling a closed-form index
calculation and what lets an embedded formulation reclassify new geometry without remeshing.
Zero means Field meshed a body itself and sent it, in which case there is no (i, j, k) to compute
from and the index-based views are unavailable.

## SimulationResult.kt { #simulationresult-kt }

One solved revision: the raw fields exactly as Kratos produced them, and the views Field draws.

The result is **described rather than declared**. The worker sends a `fields` list saying which
arrays it produced, whether each is nodal or per-cell, and how many components it has, and this
class holds whatever arrived. That is what lets one class carry a scalar temperature and a
velocity–pressure pair without knowing about either: [`named`](simulation.md#simulationresult-kt--simulationresult--named) is the general accessor, and
[`temperature`](simulation.md#simulationresult-kt--simulationresult--temperature), [`pressure`](simulation.md#simulationresult-kt--simulationresult--pressure) and [`velocity`](simulation.md#simulationresult-kt--simulationresult--velocity) are conveniences that fail with the list of fields that
*are* present rather than with a null.

Two fields follow from how the formulation meets its geometry rather than from its physics, and
they are direct properties for that reason. An **embedded** result carries [`distance`](simulation.md#simulationresult-kt--simulationresult--distance), the signed
nodal level set, positive on the side that was solved, and [`cellState`](simulation.md#simulationresult-kt--simulationresult--cellstate), `0` inactive, `1` wholly
inside, `2` cut. A **body-fitted** result carries neither: its mesh is the body, so there is no
level set to report and no cell to classify, and both accessors say which fields did arrive
rather than inventing zeros.

### Sampling is barycentric in the grid's own tetrahedra

[`sample`](simulation.md#simulationresult-kt--simulationresult--sample) finds the containing cube, sorts the local coordinates to pick the same one of the six
Freudenthal tetrahedra the worker built, and takes its four barycentric weights. It is not
trilinear hexahedral interpolation and would disagree with one; it matches the discretisation
the answer was computed on. A point outside the domain, or one with no active support, samples
as `null` rather than as zero.

That index calculation is closed-form only on a structured grid, so on a body-fitted mesh point
sampling is `null` everywhere and [`sliceMesh`](simulation.md#simulationresult-kt--simulationresult--slicemesh) refuses outright. [`boundaryMesh`](simulation.md#simulationresult-kt--simulationresult--boundarymesh) and [`deformedMesh`](simulation.md#simulationresult-kt--simulationresult--deformedmesh)
are the views to draw there.

## BoidSketch.kt { #boidsketch-kt }

Boids as a declarative spec: kinds of boid, each with a count, speed limits, a field of view, a
look and a list of Reynolds steering rules, all stepped together on the GPU over a neighbour
grid and drawn with tapered trails. The Field port of the boids page
(`~/temp/characters/boids.html`); `dev_docs/madp/boids.md` maps its `flock({...})` spec.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/particles/BoidSketch.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/particles/BoidSketch/)

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">BoidRock</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">r</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/particles/BoidSketch/#L217)

### BoidTables { #boidsketch-kt-boidtables }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">BoidTables</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">settings</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">BoidSketchSettings</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/particles/BoidSketch/#L260)

The tables a flock's spec becomes on the GPU, worked out the way the page's `flock()` works them out: each rule's `among` as a bit mask over kinds, each kind's query radius (its largest rule radius) and its reach to every kind (the largest radius of its rules that see that kind), and the grid's cell size (the most populous kind's query radius, at least 16).

### BoidSketch { #boidsketch-kt-boidsketch }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">BoidSketch</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">module</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ComputeModulePointer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renderer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Renderer</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">fromContext</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">configure</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">BoidSketchSettings</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">{</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/particles/BoidSketch/#L344)

Hosts a flock whose look is a compute shader built on `#include "boids/flock"`: the shader defines `vec4 color(Boid b)` (and `flowAngle` or the custom-rule hooks when the spec uses them), and this class does everything else: it writes the spec into the rule and kind tables, places the boids, steps them [`BoidSketchSettings.steps`](simulation.md#boidsketch-kt--boidsketchsettings--steps) times a frame at [`BoidSketchSettings.fps`](simulation.md#boidsketch-kt--boidsketchsettings--fps) over a [`GpuNeighbourGrid`](graphics.md#gpuneighbourgrid-kt-gpuneighbourgrid), keeps a 121-step history of each, and draws rocks, trails, bodies and the inspector into a [`PointAccumulation`](graphics.md#pointaccumulation-kt-pointaccumulation) faded by [`BoidSketchSettings.fade`](simulation.md#boidsketch-kt--boidsketchsettings--fade) each frame.

## IteratedSystem.kt { #iteratedsystem-kt }

Iterated systems: many particles, each stepped by the same rule every frame and plotted after
every step, so their visits pile up into the shape the rule keeps returning to — the chaos game
behind an IFS fern, the flow of a strange attractor, a fractal flame.

### IteratedSystem { #iteratedsystem-kt-iteratedsystem }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">IteratedSystem</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">module</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ComputeModulePointer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renderer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Renderer</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">fromContext</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">configure</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">IteratedSystemSettings</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">{</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/particles/IteratedSystem/#L77)

Hosts an iterated system whose rule is a compute shader built on `#include "points/system"`: the shader defines `initParticle`, `step`, `project`, `shouldDraw`, `color` and `pointSize`, and the include's `main()` steps every particle [`IteratedSystemSettings.steps`](simulation.md#iteratedsystem-kt--iteratedsystemsettings--steps) times a frame and writes a point per step. This class allocates the particle and point buffers, dispatches the shader in the box's compute module, and plots the points into a [`PointAccumulation`](graphics.md#pointaccumulation-kt-pointaccumulation) it installs on the renderer.

## ParticleSketch.kt { #particlesketch-kt }

Particle sketching on the GPU: particles you paint into the renderer window by dragging, each
moved every frame by a compute shader written against `#include "particles/sketch"`, drawn as
glowing dots with threads between them and trails behind them. The Field port of the madp
Particles demo; `dev_docs/madp/particles.md` has the mapping from its JS hooks.

### ParticleSketch { #particlesketch-kt-particlesketch }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ParticleSketch</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">module</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ComputeModulePointer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renderer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Renderer</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">fromContext</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">configure</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ParticleSketchSettings</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">{</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/particles/ParticleSketch/#L154)

Hosts a particle sketch whose behaviour is a compute shader built on `#include "particles/sketch"`. The shader defines madp's hooks as GLSL — `spawn(at)`, `eachPair(other, pair)`, `update()` and `draw()` — and this class runs them: it keeps the particles in two GPU buffers that swap every frame, rebuilds a [`GpuNeighbourGrid`](graphics.md#gpuneighbourgrid-kt-gpuneighbourgrid) over them (72-pixel cells, as madp's spatial hash), steps every particle, and draws links, dots and overlays into a [`PointAccumulation`](graphics.md#pointaccumulation-kt-pointaccumulation) that fades by `1 - trail` each frame, shown over [`ParticleSketchSettings.background`](simulation.md#particlesketch-kt--particlesketchsettings--background).

## PetriLayoutSolver.kt { #petrilayoutsolver-kt }

The force-directed layout behind `PetriLayout.FORCE`: a spring relaxation run many times from
different random starts, each scored for legibility, with the best drawing kept.

A spring model settles into *a* local minimum of its own energy, which is not the same thing as
a drawing you can read: thirty nodes of dining philosophers reach a respectable energy and still
come out as a hairball. So the energy is not the verdict. Each restart is scored on what makes a
graph legible, crossings first, then overlapping nodes, then nodes standing on an edge, and the
best-scoring drawing wins. A restart with none of the three ends the search early.

Random, but repeatable. Every restart is seeded from a hash of the net's own structure, so the
same net draws the same way on every machine and every run.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/petri/PetriLayoutSolver.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/petri/PetriLayoutSolver/)

## PetriSmokeTest.kt { #petrismoketest-kt }

The whole stack, end to end, in one headless process: model, notation, analysis, the pattern
bridge, the live runtime, the drawing, and — the part that matters most — **the sound**.

The unit tests in `src/jvmTest` pin each layer's semantics. This asserts the thing they cannot:
that a net put through the real offline voice actually produces audio with the onsets the net
says it should. "It plays" is measured here, not claimed. A net whose piano roll looks right and
whose WAV is silent would pass every unit test in the tree and fail this one.

Nothing committed is written. Pass an output directory as `args[0]` (or set `PETRI_SMOKE_DIR`) to
keep the rendered WAVs and SVGs for listening and looking at.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/petri/PetriSmokeTest.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/petri/PetriSmokeTest/)

## CSVReader.kt { #csvreader-kt }

A reader for motion-capture CSV, and a clip that samples it at an arbitrary time.

The format is one row per captured frame: a time in the first column, then three columns per
joint. Joint names come out of the header, which is expected to read
`time,Hip.x,Hip.y,Hip.z,Knee.x,…`: every third cell, cut at its first `.`. `MotionClip.load` does
that parsing and is the only way to build a clip from a file. It sits on the companion object, so
it has no row of its own on this page.

[`MotionClip`](simulation.md#csvreader-kt-motionclip) sorts its frames by time on construction, and `sample(t)` clamps `t` into the clip's
range, binary-searches for the bracketing pair of frames and interpolates every joint linearly
between them. The vectors that come back are fresh copies, so a caller can move them around
without disturbing the clip.

A clip holds no reference to a solver and nothing else in `afield.simulation.physics` reads one, so
which particle a joint drives is a decision for the calling code. Two kinds of malformed input
load without an exception. A data row with fewer fields than the header promises is skipped, so a
truncated file becomes a shorter clip; and a file whose every data row is short becomes a clip of
no frames, which answers `sample` with an empty map and throws from `start`, `end` and
`duration`.

## Cloth.kt { #cloth-kt }

A rectangular cloth patch on a [`SimdVerlet`](simulation.md#simdverlet-kt-simdverlet) simulation.

`Cloth.addTo` (or [`SimdVerlet.addCloth`](simulation.md#cloth-kt--addcloth)) appends `width * height` particles to an existing
simulation, wires their edge springs into the constraint solve, and returns a handle that
knows the grid. The handle drives the whole simulation through [`Cloth.step`](simulation.md#cloth-kt--cloth--step) or the
infinite-sequence [`Cloth.frames`](simulation.md#cloth-kt--cloth--frames), and exposes grid coordinates via [`Cloth.position`](simulation.md#cloth-kt--cloth--position),
[`Cloth.pin`](simulation.md#cloth-kt--cloth--pin) and [`Cloth.grabNearest`](simulation.md#cloth-kt--cloth--grabnearest).

## Dyn4jScene.kt { #dyn4jscene-kt }

A 2D rigid-body scene: dyn4j's `World` behind a Kotlin surface that addresses bodies by handle,
with a converter from Field's own drawing into collision geometry.

[`SimdVerlet`](simulation.md#simdverlet-kt-simdverlet) has no notion of a rigid body. Its colliders push particles out of shapes, and
nothing a particle touches is pushed back by it. This is the other half of that, flat: bodies
with mass, rotation, friction and restitution, resolving contacts against one another.
[`JoltPhysicsWorld`](simulation.md#joltphysicsworld-kt-joltphysicsworld) is the same idea in 3D, and [`SimdVerletDyn4jBridge`](simulation.md#simdverletdyn4jbridge-kt-simdverletdyn4jbridge) runs a particle
simulation and one of these scenes in the same frame.

### Handles, not bodies

[`addBody`](simulation.md#dyn4jscene-kt--dyn4jscene--addbody) returns a [`DynBodyHandle`](simulation.md#dyn4jscene-kt-dynbodyhandle) rather than the dyn4j `Body` it made, and every accessor
takes one. Handle ids count up from 1 and are never reused, so a handle to a removed body
cannot come to mean a later one. A handle whose body has been removed resolves to nothing:
[`getBodyState`](simulation.md#dyn4jscene-kt--dyn4jscene--getbodystate) returns `null`, [`removeBody`](simulation.md#dyn4jscene-kt--dyn4jscene--removebody) returns `false`, and the five mutators return
without touching anything. Nothing throws on a stale handle, which suits a `loop { }` editing a
scene it is also drawing.

[`world`](simulation.md#dyn4jscene-kt--dyn4jscene--world) is public. Joints, raycasts, contact listeners and everything else dyn4j offers are
reached through it; what this class covers is making bodies, moving them and reading them back.

### Shapes

[`DynShapeDef`](simulation.md#dyn4jscene-kt-dynshapedef) has four cases. `Box` and `Circle` go straight to dyn4j primitives. `Polygon`
must already be a convex loop, and a loop dyn4j rejects is re-reported as an `error` carrying
dyn4j's own complaint. `Concave` is decomposed by Bayazit into convex parts, and each part
becomes a fixture on the one body, so a concave body is several fixtures sharing a transform.

Both vertex cases are sanitised first: consecutive duplicates are dropped, a repeated closing
point is removed, dyn4j's own `cleanse` runs, and a loop whose signed winding is negative is
reversed, so every loop reaching dyn4j turns the same way whichever way it was drawn. Fewer
than three distinct vertices fails a `require`.

### Mass and rest

`DynBodyKind.STATIC` sets `MassType.INFINITE`; `DynBodyKind.DYNAMIC` takes its mass from
[`DynBodyDef.density`](simulation.md#dyn4jscene-kt--dynbodydef--density) and the fixture areas. Density is floored just above zero, so asking for
`0.0` gives a very light body rather than a massless one. dyn4j lets a body that has stopped
moving go to rest; every mutator here clears that flag, including the two that write
`body.transform` directly and so bypass dyn4j entirely.

[`DynBodyState.position`](simulation.md#dyn4jscene-kt--dynbodystate--position) is the body's centre of mass, while [`setBodyTransform`](simulation.md#dyn4jscene-kt--dyn4jscene--setbodytransform) writes the
transform's translation. For a box or a circle, both of which dyn4j builds around the origin,
those coincide. For a polygon given arbitrary vertices they need not, so setting a position and
reading it back does not always round-trip.

### Stepping

[`step`](simulation.md#dyn4jscene-kt--dyn4jscene--step) is one dyn4j iteration of exactly the `dtSeconds` it is given, so the timestep belongs
to the caller. Gravity defaults to zero on both axes: a scene made with no arguments is
weightless, and gravity is changed afterwards through `world.gravity`.

### FLines as collision geometry

`flattenClosedFLineLoops` turns a drawn [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) into vertex loops for `DynShapeDef.Concave` or
`Polygon`, by way of `java.awt.geom` path flattening: curves become runs of line segments at
the given tolerance and subdivision limit, and each subpath of three or more points comes back
as a loop with any duplicate closing point removed. It reads `SEG_CLOSE` off the path iterator,
but its final flush accepts an unterminated subpath as well, and a dyn4j polygon is closed
implicitly, so a line drawn without a closing node converts to the same vertices as one drawn
with it. `InteriorCloseNodeTest.theDyn4jLoopFlattenerWasNeverActuallyBroken` pins that.

Nothing else in the repository constructs a [`Dyn4jScene`](simulation.md#dyn4jscene-kt-dyn4jscene). These are a surface for box code to
call, and that one test case is the only coverage the file has.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/physics/Dyn4jScene.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/physics/Dyn4jScene/)

## JoltCameraFrustumPlanes.kt { #joltcamerafrustumplanes-kt }

Walls for what the camera can see: six static Jolt planes, kept on the view frustum as it moves.

The motivation is a sketch where things are meant to stay on screen. Six plane bodies are created
in a [`JoltPhysicsWorld`](simulation.md#joltphysicsworld-kt-joltphysicsworld), one per face and each named for its face under a shared `prefix`, with
their normals turned to face the interior. The region they close off is then exactly the volume
the camera is looking at, and a dynamic body inside it stays inside.

The frustum is derived from the camera's `fov`, `aspect` and principal-point offsets, with near
and far from the camera unless overridden. It is a perspective frustum in every case: this reads
nothing from the projection's `orthoness`, so a camera part way to orthographic gets planes that
do not match its picture.

Calling `update` every frame is cheap when nothing has moved. A plane is rebuilt only when its
normal or constant has shifted past `updateEpsilon`, or when its body has gone missing from the
world; `add` is the same function under a name that reads better the first time. After any rebuild
the world's dynamic bodies are woken, unless `wakeDynamicBodiesOnUpdate` is off, which they have
to be: a body asleep against a wall does not notice the wall moving.

Nothing in the repository calls this, in `src` or in the docs pages.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/physics/JoltCameraFrustumPlanes.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/physics/JoltCameraFrustumPlanes/)

## JoltDebugDrawing.kt { #joltdebugdrawing-kt }

Wireframes for the Jolt collision shapes: what `JoltPhysicsWorld.debugWireLines3D` is made of.

Nothing here is public, which is why this page lists no declarations for it. The file holds one
builder per case of [`JoltShape`](simulation.md#joltphysicsworld-kt-joltshape), an axes gizmo, and the transform and colour steps that follow,
all of them `internal` to [`JoltPhysicsWorld`](simulation.md#joltphysicsworld-kt-joltphysicsworld)'s use. Each builder draws in the shape's own local
space, centred on the origin, and `transformLines` is what carries the result out to a body's
pose.

The drawings are outlines rather than meshes, because they are there to be seen through while
something else is rendered inside them. A sphere is three great circles, not a tessellation. A
capsule is a ring at each end, a ring at the waist when there is a cylinder to have one, and two
stadium profiles at right angles. An infinite plane becomes a square patch around the point on it
nearest the origin, with a stub along the normal, which points away from the solid side.

`colorForBodyName` hashes the name and lifts each channel away from black, which is what keeps a
body the same colour from run to run without anyone choosing one.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/physics/JoltDebugDrawing.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/physics/JoltDebugDrawing/)

## JoltPhysicsBootstrap.kt { #joltphysicsbootstrap-kt }

Getting the jolt-jni native library loaded, which has to happen once per JVM before any Jolt call.

The library ships inside the jar as a per-platform resource, under an `os/arch` directory pair
followed by `com/github/stephengold/` and the platform's own filename, so there is nothing to
install and nothing to put on `java.library.path`. A JNI library cannot be loaded from inside a
jar, so the resource is copied to a temporary directory first and the copy is what gets loaded.
Point `-Dafield.joltjni.library` or the `AFIELD_JOLTJNI_LIBRARY` environment variable at an
absolute path to skip the copy and load a library you built yourself.

Both halves of that directory pair are tables, over `os.name` and `os.arch`: macOS, Windows or
Linux, on aarch64 or x86-64. A platform in neither table fails here, naming the two properties it
read, rather than at the first native call.

The only caller is the constructor of [`JoltPhysicsWorld`](simulation.md#joltphysicsworld-kt-joltphysicsworld), which runs this on every world it
builds; the second and later calls return immediately.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/physics/JoltPhysicsBootstrap.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/physics/JoltPhysicsBootstrap/)

## JoltPhysicsWorld.kt { #joltphysicsworld-kt }

Rigid bodies in three dimensions, from the Jolt physics engine: the 3D counterpart to
[`Dyn4jScene`](simulation.md#dyn4jscene-kt-dyn4jscene), and a different tool from [`SimdVerlet`](simulation.md#simdverlet-kt-simdverlet), which has no notion of a rigid body at all.

A body here is a **name**. `createBody` takes a [`JoltBodyDef`](simulation.md#joltphysicsworld-kt-joltbodydef) carrying a string name, a
[`JoltShape`](simulation.md#joltphysicsworld-kt-joltshape) and a pose, and everything afterwards addresses that body by the same string:
`applyImpulse("crate", …)`, `mass("crate")`, `removeBody("ground")`. Names are unique, and
creating a body over a name that already exists removes the old one first, so re-running a box
that builds a scene rebuilds it rather than stacking a second copy on top. `step` hands back one
[`JoltBodyState`](simulation.md#joltphysicsworld-kt-joltbodystate) per body, named the same way.

Nothing from the jolt-jni bindings reaches any of those signatures. Shapes, poses and velocities
are Field's own `Vec3` and `Quat`, the four cases of [`JoltShape`](simulation.md#joltphysicsworld-kt-joltshape) are the whole shape vocabulary,
and the conversions both ways are private at the bottom of this file. The native library loads
itself on the first world built ([`JoltPhysicsBootstrap`](simulation.md#joltphysicsbootstrap-kt-joltphysicsbootstrap)).

Two facts about what counts as static: a `JoltShape.Plane` is static whatever its `dynamic` flag
says, since an infinite plane has no volume to take a mass from, and collision filtering has
exactly two object layers, moving and non-moving, with the non-moving pair disabled. So "static"
means either `dynamic = false` or a plane, and nothing static is ever tested against anything
else static.

`pickBodyNearPoint` asks Jolt nothing. It walks the named bodies and solves point-to-surface in
closed form for a cuboid, a sphere and a capsule, so the distance it reports is *signed*, with
negative meaning the query point is inside the body. Planes are skipped, which is usually what
you want: a click near the ground finds the crate on it and not the ground. `pickAndBeginRigidGrab`
is that search and `beginRigidGrab` in one call, for a controller that has just closed.

The wireframes `debugWireLines3D` returns are built in `JoltDebugDrawing.kt`, one set of `FLine`s
per shape kind. Evaluating a world, a [`JoltBodyState`](simulation.md#joltphysicsworld-kt-joltbodystate) or a [`JoltBodyPick`](simulation.md#joltphysicsworld-kt-joltbodypick) in a box shows a
formatted summary instead of a `toString`, which `registerJoltPhysicsVisualizers` installs.

The `*3D`-suffixed typealiases at the bottom of the file, and [`JoltBodyDef`](simulation.md#joltphysicsworld-kt-joltbodydef)'s `x`/`y`/`z`
secondary constructor, are an earlier spelling of all of this and are deprecated in place; new
code uses the unprefixed names and `position: Vec3`.

## OctreeBarnesHut.kt { #octreebarneshut-kt }

Approximate inverse-square forces over a particle cloud, by summarising distant groups as a
single mass each.

Every particle acting on every other one is a quadratic sum. Barnes-Hut trades a bounded error
for `n log n`: build an octree over the positions, give each node the total mass and centre of
mass of everything beneath it, then walk the tree once per particle and stop at any node that
subtends a small enough angle, using its summary instead of descending into it.
[`OctreeBarnesHut`](simulation.md#octreebarneshut-kt-octreebarneshut) is that, over separate `x`/`y`/`z` `FloatArray`s, which is the layout
[`SimdVerlet`](simulation.md#simdverlet-kt-simdverlet) holds its state in, though the solver itself never calls this.
[`OctreeBarnesHutPool`](simulation.md#octreebarneshut-kt-octreebarneshutpool) hands out reusable instances.

A step is two calls, `build` then `applyForces`, and the masses the second one uses are the ones
the first captured. `applyForces` accumulates into the acceleration arrays with `+=`, so what it
computes adds to whatever the caller has already written there.

The kernel is `g * m / r²` along the vector from the particle to a node's centre of mass, which
makes the sign of `g` the choice of what the law is for. Positive attracts, and is gravity;
negative repels, which is how a force-directed graph layout uses one of these to avoid comparing
every pair of nodes. `theta` sets how rough the answer is: zero descends all the way to
individual particles and is the exact pairwise sum, larger values accept more summarised nodes
and do less work. `softening` is added in quadrature to the distance, bounding the force at
short range so that a near-coincidence does not produce an arbitrarily large acceleration.

The node arrays grow by half again when they must and are never handed back, and `clear` only
resets the node count, so a tree rebuilt every frame allocates nothing on the serial build path.
The parallel path allocates its eight octant index arrays per `build`. Mutation, meaning `build`
and `clear`, is not thread-safe. A parallel `applyForces` is, because each worker takes its
traversal stack from a `ThreadLocal`; the serial path instead uses the one stack it shares with
`forEachCuboid`.

Particles are separated by comparing a coordinate against a node's centre, so two at exactly the
same position fall into the same child at every depth and subdivision has nothing to terminate
on. Jitter coincident inputs before building.

## PointController.kt { #pointcontroller-kt }

PointDriver -- position in, force out.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val drv = PointDriver(DriverConfig(dt = 1.0 / 120.0, worldScale = 1.0))
drv.grab(target)                     // may be called every frame; target can move
val f = drv.update(pos)              // per frame, fixed dt
drv.releaseGrab()                    // then keep calling update() -- see below
```

Vectors are Field's ordinary Vector3f; every scalar the controller reasons
about -- gains, timescales, the identified plant -- stays Double. The file is otherwise standalone.

The whole controller state lives in the instance, so a rune-keyed slot holding
one PointDriver per particle survives hot-reload with the learned plant model
intact. Nothing needs re-priming except omega, which re-converges in ~1s.

### What it does, in four coupled timescales

 1. ~dt      model-inverting PD+I on acceleration, output through a
    bounded-curvature force limiter (magnitude, magnitude rate, and
    angular rate/acceleration on the direction).
 2. ~100ms   discrete-time RLS identification of the host's own integrator:
        x(k+1) - 2x(k) + x(k-1) = dt^2 (b F(k) + c v(k) + d)
    exact under semi-implicit Euler, so b^ absorbs the host's
    numerical damping and dispersion, not just the mass. Gains are
    synthesised from (b,c,d); the only free knobs are physical.
 3. ~seconds omega hunting driven by sin(lagAngle) -- the direction-limiter's
    turn-rate deficit. Slow rise, fast knockback: self-organised
    criticality that pins omega to the capture/orbit bifurcation.
 4. ~10s     winding memory in the limiter's rotation axis. Chirality flips
    become rare punctuated events with heavy-tailed dwell times.

### Position-only input, done properly

 - Velocity comes from the host's delta-position, which is the average over
   the interval and therefore centred at t - dt/2. Corrected by extrapolating
   dt/2 forward through the identified model -- pure phase recovery, no noise
   amplification. Uncorrected this donates omega*dt/2 of lag straight to the
   limiter and lowers the bandwidth ceiling.
 - TWO velocity signals, never crossed:
        vHat  (model observer)  -> control law only
        vPrev (raw, prefiltered) -> identifier only
   Feeding the observer estimate to the identifier is circular -- it was built
   from the force and the current model, so the RLS would confirm whatever it
   already believes. That failure looks stable for minutes, then diverges.
 - Jump guard: a single-frame teleport or collision reads as enormous velocity.
   Rejected on a running speed estimate; the identifier skips two frames while
   the second-difference window refills, and the model is left untouched.
 - Identification freezes while the limiter is saturated. If the host solves
   springs as constraints (PBD/XPBD, fixed iterations) the effective stiffness
   depends on how hard we are pushing, which makes b^ a function of our own
   aggression -- a self-referential loop that can actually diverge. Freezing
   plus a slow forgetting factor breaks it.
 - Release ramps magnitude to zero and FREEZES the aim, and keeps identifying
   through the ringdown. Free modal data with no control input to confound it,
   and the retained aim couples successive grabs.

## ShaderBoids.kt { #shaderboids-kt }

Reynolds boids as a Vulkan compute shader, over a GPU neighbour grid, with the interaction rule
swappable for a trained network.

Two declarations. [`BoidSettings`](simulation.md#shaderboids-kt-boidsettings) carries the three classical weights, the speed limit, and two
forcing terms that contribute nothing until they are turned on. [`ShaderBoids`](simulation.md#shaderboids-kt-shaderboids) owns one storage
buffer of particles, generates the GLSL that steps them, and installs the grid rebuild and the
rule into one ordered target map, in the order those two have to run.

### One system, three rules

With neither `learned` nor `equivariant` set it computes the classical three-term force in
hand-written GLSL. Given [`DeepSetsWeights`](machine-learning.md#deepsets-kt-deepsetsweights) it evaluates a trained sum-then-combine network at
the same place in the same neighbour loop, and given [`EquivariantWeights`](machine-learning.md#deepsets-kt-equivariantweights) it evaluates the
rotation-equivariant form. The buffer, the neighbour walk, the speed limit and the integration
are the same code in all three cases, so changing that one argument compares rules rather than
implementations. Passing both fails at construction.

### Sized to the grid

The neighbour query is the 3x3 block of cells around a particle's own, which reaches one cell
width in each direction, so `BoidSettings.radius` cannot exceed the grid's `cellSize`. A radius
that does not fit still produces something that looks like a flock, computed from a subset of
each particle's neighbours, so `install` checks it. The particle count has to fit the grid's
capacity, and the constructor checks that.

### Graded against a CPU oracle

`referenceAcceleration` is the same law in Kotlin over every other particle, and
`four.shader-boids.smoke` compares the two per particle, for a uniform flock and for a
clustered one. It runs them with `dt = 0`, where nothing moves and the accelerations are a
fixed function of a fixed configuration; boids is chaotic, so two trajectories compared after a
few hundred steps would measure how fast they separate and not whether the two implement the
same law. The force each particle
stores is the interaction alone, written before the containment and driver terms are added and
before the velocity is integrated.

### Drawing it

`installDrawInto` adds a point-list pass that reads the same allocation the compute pass wrote,
with no copy, tinting from slow colour to fast colour by speed. The point the driver term pulls
toward comes from a lambda the push bindings call every frame, so a box can move it without
re-running anything.

The prose, with pictures: [Neural particle systems](../neural_particles.md).
